lines.text: Once one of the poorest countries on Earth, now a steady democracy built on diamonds and good sense. This is the story of Botswana.
In 1837 Khama the Third was born. As king of the Bamangwato he would turn to Britain to protect his people from the Boers.
In 1885 Britain agreed, and the land became the Bechuanaland Protectorate, which it stayed for some eighty years.
Khama's grandson Seretse was born in 1921. His marriage to an Englishwoman caused a scandal, but he would become the nation's first president.
Quett Masire, born in 1925, would follow him, and lead the country for almost two decades.
Festus Mogae, born in 1939, would be the president who led Botswana's fight against HIV.
In 1965 a new capital, Gaborone, was built for the coming independence.
In 1966 Botswana was born, one of the poorest countries in the world, but one that would become one of Africa's most stable democracies.
Two years later the government and De Beers went into diamonds together. Their company, Debswana, would change everything.
In 1969 Duma Boko was born. Decades later, the lawyer would lead the opposition to a historic win.
In 1971 the Orapa mine opened, on diamonds found just after independence. Botswana's wealth had begun.
In 2014 the Okavango Delta, a vast green fan of water in the Kalahari, was listed as a World Heritage Site.
And in 2024 voters ended fifty eight years of rule by one party, and power passed peacefully to Duma Boko.
Botswana shows how a small, quiet nation can turn good fortune into lasting peace.
